source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC3805449 (abstract, Introduction, Methods, Discussion and Recommendations with all subsections and the four illustrative cases, Conclusions, Appendices A-C), read in my own browser tab

claims.overstatement: Minor: the claim puts it in the present tense ('common screening tests miss'); it is a 2013 consensus statement about immunoassays of that time, not a measurement, and screening methods have changed since. The claim correctly attributes it to the panel.
claims.note: 'Common screening tests' = immunoassays, which the panel names as the usual first step (immunoassay, then GC-MS confirmation of presumptive positives). The panel adds that the lack of standard practice may lead to underreporting of prescription opioids in deaths, which supports the claim's 'what is tested changes what is found'. The same subsection notes wide variation between death investigation systems in routine toxicology standards.

anchors.locator: Discussion and Recommendations > Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Immunoassays vary in what they detect; many miss toxicologically significant opiates, especially oxycodone and hydromorphone; laboratories use no standard threshold of detection; the panel says the lack of standard practice may lead to underreporting of prescription opioids in deaths.

anchors.locator: Discussion and Recommendations > Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Standards of practice for routine toxicology vary significantly across medicolegal death investigation systems; the most common approach is an immunoassay screen of urine with GC-MS confirmation of presumptive positives.

claims.note: Both points are in the source. Coding: the panel lists phrases coded as poisoning X42 with T40.5 (acute cocaine intoxication or toxicity, toxic effects of cocaine, cocaine poisoning, cocaine overdose) against phrases coded F14, mental and behavioural disorders due to cocaine (cocaine use, abuse, snorting, addiction). Caused versus detected: three case definitions (drug-caused, drug-poisoning subcategory, drug-detected). The man shot dead is the panel's illustrative Case 3, not a real case; there his toxicology showed a potentially lethal drug concentration and he was still classed drug-detected only, which makes the claim's point more strongly than 'a drug in his blood'. The panel's drug-poisoning definition lists the same underlying-cause codes as the US counts (X40-X44, X60-X64, X85, Y10-Y14), while its drug-caused definition (parallel to NCHS 'drug-induced') also takes in chronic effects, adverse reactions and mental and behavioural disorders, another instance of different counts counting different things.

anchors.locator: Discussion and Recommendations > Determination and Documentation of Causality > Documenting Causality on the Death Certificate, 6th paragraph (10th of the section)
anchors.extracted: The wording of the cause of death decides whether vital statistics classify the death as an acute poisoning or a chronic condition: acute cocaine intoxication, acute cocaine toxicity, toxic effects of cocaine, cocaine poisoning and cocaine overdose are coded poisoning X42 with T40.5; cocaine use, cocaine abuse, cocaine snorting and cocaine addiction are coded F14 (mental and behavioural disorders due to use of cocaine).

anchors.locator: Discussion and Recommendations > Case Definitions, items 1, 1-a and 2
anchors.extracted: Drug-caused death: certified as resulting from drug exposure, any intent; includes chronic effects, adverse reactions and mental and behavioural disorders due to drugs; parallels NCHS 'drug-induced deaths'. Drug-poisoning death (subcategory): acute exposure, equivalent to the lay idea of overdose; parallels underlying cause X40-X44, X60-X64, X85, Y10-Y14. Drug-detected death: drug found on post-mortem testing whatever its role, including natural and traumatic deaths; maps to no ICD-10 code set.

anchors.locator: Discussion and Recommendations > Determination and Documentation of Causality > Case 3: Homicide with a History of Drug Use
anchors.extracted: Illustrative case: a 22-year-old man dies of gunshot wounds to the head; toxicology shows a potentially lethal drug concentration; cause of death gunshot wounds; drug-caused no, drug-poisoning no, drug-detected yes, because an independent intervening process caused the death.

Earlier SAMHSA expert meetings (2003, 2007, 2010) concluded that medical examiners and coroners do not appear to use common definitions for opioid-caused deaths, and theirs may differ from those used on death certificates, making data hard to compare; the panel was charged to separate deaths caused by a drug from deaths in which it was detected but was not a major cause or contributor.

claims.note: The source is firmer than the claim on medical examiners: it states that they are professionally trained forensic pathologists in appointed positions (no 'usually'); the claim's hedge is not from this source. On coroners the source says 'generally' elected or appointed. It adds that coroners who are not physicians must use coroners' physicians for autopsies. These are the panel's definitions (Appendix B), not survey data, and the panel makes no comparison of how the two systems count deaths.

anchors.locator: Appendix B. Recommended Terminology > Medical Examiner and Coroner
anchors.extracted: Medical examiner: the government entity responsible for medicolegal death investigation that certifies cause and manner of death; medical examiners are professionally trained forensic pathologists in appointed positions. Coroner: the original US system, from England; generally elected or appointed officials with widely varying qualifications; those who are not physicians must use coroners' physicians for autopsies; some can still hold inquests.
The premise is that medical examiners and coroners alike lack common definitions for opioid-caused deaths; the panel does not compare the two systems.
